Contrary to the headline ECI result which was driven by incentive-paid occupations, today's quarterly wage data is consistent with a continued slowdown in wage growth towards 2% core inflation-consistent levels. 
#NumbersDay

Using paleoproteomics (ZooMS), my team identified a tiny hominin skull fragment at Riparo Bombrini (Level M4), in the Balzi Rossi site complex in NW Italy. Its age and cultural association material of the layer (43.5k cal. years BP, Mousterian tools) mean it's very likely a Neanderthal. 🏺🧪

The Iron Crown of Lombardy was made in the Middle Ages. Legend maintains its central band was beaten from a nail of the True Cross. It was used in the coronation of the first Holy Roman Emperor Charlemagne on Christmas day 800 and was worn again in 1805 by Napoleon when he was crowned King of Italy.

Mausoleum of the Julii situated in Glanum, a Roman village in s. France, modern St.Rémy-de-Provence, c. 40 BC.

Architrave inscription: 
SEX · M · L · IVLIEI · C · F · PARENTIBVS · SVEIS 
Sextius, Marcus and Lucius Julius, sons of Gaius, to their forebears.

Credit Lauren Heilman 
🏺 Ancientbluesky

This magnificent Gallic flagon dates to c450 BCE. It’s exquisitely cast & regarded as a masterpiece of early Celtic art. If you look closely at the spout, there’s even a little joke at work as there’s a bronze duck who will ride the flow of beer or wine as it’s poured out

🏛️BM 📷me
🏺 AncientBlueSky

"There is no altar anywhere in England, nor has there been any abroad, so handsomely adorned," wrote John Evelyn of the beautiful lime wood carvings of Grinling Gibbons, who was dubbed the "King Carver" of the late 17th century, on the altar of Christopher Wren's 1684 church, St James Piccadilly.

#MosaicMonday - Discovered 8 March 1764 in the 'Villa of Cicero'. A grand mosaic (dubbed 'The Sorceress'), signed by Dioskourides of Samos, likely representing a scene from Comedy. #Pompeii 🏺ClassicsBluesky 

Image: National Archaeological Museum, Naples (9987). Link - mann-napoli.it/mosaici/#gal...

1st c. CE Roman terracotta from Syria, depicting two female musicians on a camel. They each hold a tympanum, a hand drum. If you look closely, you can see traces of bright pink pigment that once decorated their shared cloak. #polychromy 

Princeton University Art Museum (y1952-53) 🏺

Carts are a frequent topic on Late Geometric Greek vessels, as part of funeral ceremonies and as vehicles of warriors. Models of carts are rarer and this one with four horses driven by a warrior with a shield is exceptionally well preserved. 750-740 BCE, from Athens. KHM Vienna. 🏺

Stein's Pillar, Oregon
A 350 foot tall (106 m) volcanic remnant composed of tuff (ash and ejecta from an eruption), welded together, and eroded over about 40 million years after the caldera it came from has largely vanished. Probably from the Yellowstone hot spot.

Tonight's goodnight image. Escomb Church, County Durham, England. The 2nd oldest intact building in all the British Isles. Built ~AD670 from stones pilfered from the nearby Roman fort at Binchester, including a complete arch and a stone marked by the Sixth Legion.

The vibe inside is amazing. 🏺

On my recent trip to Scotland I made a special visit to the Meffan Museum in Forfar to see this lovely little bronze bust of Minerva. She was discovered at the site of a Roman fort at Cardean and dates from the early 80s AD. I particularly love the very grumpy looking Gorgon on her armour!

Last June at camp in Algoma, I saw a peculiar Phoebe; pinkish-red in colour. It turns out it was the first record of diet-induced aberrant plumage (erythrism) in this species. The editor of ABA's Birding magazine invited me to write an article, which was just published. #birds #birding

What does a chickadee look for in a home? How about northern flicker, or a purple martin? The 1923 University of North Dakota bulletin "Houses for North Dakota Birds" instructed kids how to build bird houses customized to each species they might hope to attract. 🪶🗃️

“The exceptional warming that we’re experiencing is not something we’ve seen before in human history,” said Gavin Schmidt, director of GISS. “It’s driven primarily by our fossil fuel emissions, and we’re seeing the impacts in heat waves, intense rainfall, and coastal flooding.”

"In Texas, wind and solar cut the average wholesale electricity price by 26% in 2022, saving households and businesses $11 billion...The state has increased the share of renewables in its electricity mix from 10% in 2013 to 32% in 2022." 

Clean energy is being driven by favorable economics.

September is the month when Arctic sea ice reaches its annual minimum and Antarctic sea ice reaches its maximum. Arctic monthly ice extent was the 5th lowest on record (for September). Antarctic monthly ice extent was the lowest on record (for September). Data: NSIDC and OSI SAF

The poorest 50% - 4 billion people - live on less than $6.70 a day

All measures are adjusted for differences in purchasing power.
The Fed's preferred Core PCE price index has been 2.0% annualized for two straight quarters, a return to the Fed's target with almost clinical accuracy after two years of high inflation.

I wrote about this fancy sandwich. It's a crispy hash brown patty, custardy square of egg, melty gouda, bacon, pepper jelly, and pickled onion aioli sandwiched between one of my home-baked soft potato buns. Go read about it here: boundedbybuns.com/go-go-breakf...

After many decades trying to perfect home made rotisserie chicken my 2 cents.
1. It doesn't matter what spice mix you use.
2. Use more salt than you think you should
3. Forget about slow cooker, sous vide, perfect oven.
4. Use a chicken brick. Roemertopf. Clay pot.
5. Reread 4 and act accordingly.🍜🍽️

Duck fat fries with garlic dip. (Dip’s a little fresh garlic, chipotle sauce, and 50/50 mayo/Greek yogurt.) 🍜🍽️

Made in the air fryer. Secret is: starchy potato cut thinner, & soaked in cold water, with a rinse. Dry them well before fat/cooking, & brush w more fat 3/4 through cooking them.

Lunch with friends today…happy jewel salad.

Freekeh based with loads of fresh herb, dill, parsley, mint & coriander.  A dressing of warmed olive oil melting grated garlic, then chopped sour cherries, red wine vinegar, Dijon mustard, lemon zest & juice.  Then loads of pistachios, pomegranate + feta

Potatoes were cultivated by indigenous people across the Americas, but likely 1st domesticated in the Andes region of Peru 7-10,000 years ago from wild species Solanum brevicaule.

Cultivated potatoes are all tetraploid, while wild potatoes can be diploid, tetraploid, or hexaploid.

Rhododendron loranthiflorum, an epiphytic vireya species from the Solomon Islands. Nocturnally scented white flowers suggest moth pollination.  Some clones are very compact, but my plant is long and lanky. Not sure what’s up with the species name—flowers don’t look much like a Loranthus to me. 🌱

In 1960, David Latimer planted a garden inside of a bottle and sealed it shut. He opened the bottle and watered the plant in 1972 and sealed it for good. It has been a self sustaining ecosystem for 60 years.

The Texas mountain laurels are officially in full bloom! Not a true mountain laurel, it’s a small shrub-like evergreen in the pea family endemic to central and west Texas through northern Mexico. Their blooming season (March through April) fills the air with a STRONG smell resembling grape soda! 🌿

#FridayFlower Raoulia bryoides is a large firm cushion plant from the New Zealand mountains, often called a vegetable sheep. This at 1700 m in Nelson Lakes National Park last Wednesday. The flowers are in tiny heads, showing that this is a daisy (Family Asteraceae). I invited the ladybug for scale.

I'm sorry to tell you again, but fire increases the germination of Cistaceae seeds in contrast to summer-type heat (which reduces germination!)
Paper: fireecology.springeropen.com/articles/10.... Blog: jgpausas.blogs.uv.es/2024/02/18/s...

🧪🌍🔥🌿🌾 wildfire botany #PlantBiology #PlantScience

"WVU is...the state’s major land-grant institution as well as its public flagship. While closures, cutbacks, and hiring freezes have become routine, the spectacle of a state giving up on its flagship university—for that is what these cuts amount to—is something new."

A protostar embedded in a protoplanetary disk embedded in the dark molecular cloud LDN1527. You’re seeing an infant (100,000 years old) solar system about 447 light years away. The star itself is hidden from view by the edge-on protoplanetary disk occupying the ‘neck’ of the hourglass shaped nebula.

(16) Psyche was discovered by Annibale de Gasparis at Napoli in 1852; the 22-petatonne asteroid is about 220 km across and its heliocentric orbit is 2.53 x 3.32 AU x 3.1 deg. NASA's Psyche probe is scheduled to reach Psyche in 2029.

OSIRIS-REX was launched in Sep 2016 on an Atlas V rocket from Canaveral to a 0.78 x 1.17 AU solar orbit; it arrived at asteroid (101955) Bennu in Oct 2018, collected samples in Oct 2020, and departed Bennu for the return trip to Earth in Apr 2021. Welcome home O-REX!

Here's the light curves of 1635 supernovae measured in four colours.  They brighten and fade in a couple of months, but their peak brightness is always about the same -- allowing us to use them as standard candles to measure the acceleration of the expansion of the Universe.

NGC 2392, a planetary nebula in Gemini (much brighter than yesterday's offering). Here, I've imaged it through a diffraction grating to show that the light of the planetary is almost entirely emitted by two spectral lines (blue OIII and deep red H-alpha). Stars emit a continuum.  #astrophotography

Spain’s World Cup-winning women's soccer team agreed to play their scheduled high-profile matches in the coming days. Their playing was uncertain after many demanded an overhaul of its soccer federation to promise a “safe place where women are respected.”

In 1995, Bowling Green defeated Rice 31-24 in the first and to date only Brad Dourif Bowl. It was played in Altadena, CA and sponsored by the character actor Brad Dourif (One Flew Over The Cuckoo's Nest, Child's Play). He has left open the option of sponsoring another one but to date has not.

The cathedral of St Mary, Limerick, is also home to the only complete set of misericords to survive from medieval Ireland. These beautifully carved hinged oak seats, dating from the 15th century, were designed to give support to clergy who had to stand during long services.
Details of one of the T columns in Göbekli Tepe, Turkey. It is approximately 12,000 years old, making it remarkably older than Egyptian Pyramids and Stonehenge.

The Madrague de Giens is a Roman shipwreck off the coast of S France, sinking mid C1stBCE. It was a huge merchant ship, 40m in length. Fully laden it could hold 520 tons of cargo. The amphorae found held wine, oil & other goods like garum. Its discovery was also a breakthrough in marine archaeology

Around 2,200 years ago, the artist Hephaistion left his signature on a mosaic floor in the form of a piece of parchment held down with small drops of wax. This perfect imitation of a sheet of parchment, with one corner curled up, was discovered in one of the palaces at Pergamon.

Thonis-Heraklion was founded in C8thBCE at the Nile’s mouth. Before Alexandria’s creation, it was the major port of the delta. Succeeding earthquakes & floods saw the city slip under the waves in C2ndBCE eventually disappearing c.900CE. It has been excavated since 1933
📷Franck Goddio🏺 AncientBlueSky

2,300 years old, this astonishingly life-like bronze head of Thracian king Seuthes III ~ with alabaster & glass paste eyes (bloodshot!), copper strip eyelashes & eyebrows, & maybe evidence of old injury to cheekbone (Nat Mus Archaeology, Sofia) Photo: Krasimir Georgiev

This is the Temple of Apollo in Syracuse. It was constructed in the C6th BCE in the Doric style and is one of the first temples in Sicily with a peripteros (a colonnade of columns surrounding the inner sanctuary). Like many ruined classical temples, it’s the haunt of cats. 

📷 mine
🏺 AncientBlueSky

More than forty archaeological sites in Cyprus dating potentially as far back as the Bronze Age that were thought lost to history have been relocated by University of Leicester scientists working for the Ministry of Defence. le.ac.uk/news/2024/ma...

At first glance you might think that this alabaster tomb might be from Westminster Abbey but this remarkable monument to Alice Chaucer is at St. Mary, Ewelme in Oxfordshire. She was the grandaughter of Geoffrey Chaucer. Note the stone cadaver behind the tracery at the bottom.

This is believed to be the oldest depiction of Jesus.

The 'Alexamenos graffito' (singular of graffiti), is trolling a Roman soldier named Alexamenos, apparently a Christian, likely around 200 AD.

A man is shown worshiping a donkey-headed god on a crucifix.

Text: "Alexamenos worships [his] God"

About 80 % of students thought this was a swanky straw hat from the 1950s. Truth is that it’s the oldest Roman grasswork "Panama hat" extant, from Fayum in Egypt. In 2017 they radiocarbon dated it to 420-568 CE. Turns out the “Dark Ages” was really more about cool shade (Pitt Rivers Museum, UK) 🎩

It’s Trier (or Augusta Treverorum) in western Germany. Here the Porta Nigra (started 170), the Aula Palatina (early 4th century), the imperial baths (also early 4th century) & the amphitheatre (mid-2nd century). Incredible remains.

📷 all open source
🏺 AncientBlueSky

This reticulated beaker has an inscription in glass letters: FAVENTIBVS. It’s an expression of good luck (perhaps short for "Faventibus ventis" – with favourable winds). The ‘cage’ of the beaker is also glass. These items are the pinnacle of Roman glass craft

🏛️📷Kunsthistoriches 
🏺 AncientBlueSky

The Iron Age wooden roadway at Corlea 1, Co Longford, dated to 148/147 BC. Truly a “Colossus of Roads” (I dug on this as a student, and was also at the Exeter conference where Barry tried out his dreadful pun for the first time 🥰) 🏺#Ireland #Archaeology

For EpigraphyTuesday: the funerary inscription of Julia Peiris, an obstetrix (midwife) who 'did no harm.' Notably, the first T of obstetrix is shoehorned in between the S and E. Dated to the 1st century CE, from Trier. Now in the Rheinisches Landesmuseum Trier.

AncientBlueSky 🏺

Decorative mosiac column from the  Temple of Ninhursag at Tell Al-'Ubaid, Iraq. Originally made of palm wood, coated with bitumen. Inlays of mother-of-pearl, pink limestone, and black shale were held in place by  twisted copper wires. Dated to c. 2500 BCE. 

MosiacMonday
AncientBlueSky 🏺

📷BM

Paisley Abbey was first built in the 12th century. In 1991, it underwent some necessary restoration work as 12 of its 13 gargoyles were so badly ruined from water damage they had to be removed. One stone mason had a little fun & one gargoyle bears a strong resemblance to the Xenomorph from Alien

This is an incredible relic from Ancient Rome. The bronze doors of the Lateran Cathedral (left) were originally the doors of the Senate house (right). They date to the reign of Domitian (81-96CE) & were moved to their current location in 1660 by Pope Alexander VII

📷mine 
🏺 ClassicsBlueSky

Most 3rd-4th c. CE Roman gold glass depicted Christian scenes. However, this piece depicts the god Oceanus reclining in the sea, indicated by wavy lines in pale-blue pigment. He holds a jar from which water pours; above are the legs of horses that probably pulled a chariot over the waves. #MetMuseum

This is a really lovely, but melancholy piece. It’s an Etruscan sarcophagus lid (lateC4th-early C3rd BCE) showing a touching, naturalistic representation of a middle aged husband and wife. They lie in bed, toes poking out, holding each other tenderly. Only death will part them

🏛️📷 Boston MFA

Cassin’s Finch brings #BirdGlamour to conifer & quaking aspen forests in western North America! Similar to the House Finch but with a pointier crown, Cassin’s Finches are excellent mimics and add other species’ songs to theirs. They’re also a bit salty: they love salt and visit mineral deposits. 🐡🧪🐦

Some Alberta microgeneration data: when I installed my solar panels in August of 2017, there were just under 2000 small solar installations in Alberta, with a total capacity of less than 20MW. Today, there are 14,543 sites and over 180MW of installed capacity from small solar in the province.

Wage growth held mostly steady in this quarter's employment cost index—the most in-depth measure of wages in the US.

Private sector wages grew a slightly lower 4.5% over the last year and at a slightly higher 4.3% annualized rate over the last quarter

America's prime-age employment rate—the share of 25-54-year-olds with a job—just hit the highest levels since April 2001! 

Still a lot of work to do to catch up to our previous record highs or to match the employment rates of our foreign peers, but this is incredible progress.

Local cheeses from Piedmont Italy.
Top: Robiola di Rocaverno, a soft ripened goat cheese. Less salty and creamier than, say, the Loire Valley goat cheeses that most American goat cheeses are modeled on.
Bottom: Mataronne, a mild, nutty cow's milk cheese.

JWST confirmed the redshift of the extremely distant galaxy GLASS-z12 to z=12.342.
This finding places it to be the 5th most distant galaxy ever discovered, existing only 360 Myr after the Big Bang.
arxiv.org/abs/2403.102...
🔭 🧪

The most energetic single particle ever detected, a cosmic ray dubbed the "Oh-My-God" particle, was observed by the Fly's Eye Cosmic Ray Detector OTD in 1991.

Its energy was about 3.2 x 10²⁰ eV ~ 51 J, equivalent to a baseball moving at almost 60 mph. 🧪 🔭

Image: Olena Shmahalo/Quanta Magazine

Supernovae forge a Moon's worth of gold, but kilonovae, born from neutron star collisions, churn out a Jupiter's worth! Despite our galaxy seeing ~100-1000x more SN than KN, KN contribute >10x more gold!
Your gold ring? A cosmic treasure made of stuff forged in the hearts of colliding neutron stars.

Ingenious descent profile of the first soft-landing on the surface of the Moon, Luna-9, in 1966, where the lander was encased in a pressurized 'balloon,' which bounced several times on the Moon before splitting into 2 halves and then releasing the spacecraft which then deployed all its instruments.

Look at these fab plots showing SN flux light curves from the new DES paper, showcasing 1500 new high redshift type Ia supernovae. 

Aust. astronomers, led by the excellent Prof. Tamara Davis, made big contributions! 

Universe might be ~100 million years younger 👀

📸 arxiv.org/abs/2401.02929 🔭🧪

Eta Carinae lies in the center of the Homunculus Nebula. A star on the verge of supernova, it initially went through a "Great Eruption" in the mid 1800s that ejected stellar gases and formed the nebula seen here. It is the only star known to emit natural LASER light, here in the ultraviolet spectrum

Basalt carved statue of a standing lion from the Sumerian city of Eridu, dated to the mid 3rd millennium BCE. Eridu is thought to be the earliest city built by the Sumerians, founded c. 5400 BCE on the southern marshes of the Euphrates River, Iraq. #AncientSiteSunday AncientBlueSky 🏺

Evidence for long-distance trade in the Irish Neolithic. These beautiful green jadeite axes from Donegal & Westmeath are c. 6000 years old. Studies have shown that the stone they are fashioned out of comes from a series of Neolithic quarries located high in the Italian alps

#OnThisDay in 9 BC, the Ara Pacis Augustae (Altar of Augustan Peace) in Rome is consecrated by Augustus. It had been commissioned by the Roman Senate four years earlier in celebration of Augustus' return to Rome after three years in Hispania and Gaul.

Historic storm surge at 11:48 am in Boston (data since 1921): 4th highest water level on record, 4.13’ above MHHW (record: 4.89’, 1/4/2018). Boston also had its 9th highest water level just 3 days ago. Without sea level rise of ~12” since 1921, today’s flood would rank #9. (corrected from earlier)

Rubin Observatory will measure the ghostly glow of innumerable stars stripped from their home galaxies and left to wander vast intergalactic space. Such "intracluster light" will help us understand the elusive dark matter known to pervade galaxy clusters rubinobservatory.org/news/fossil-...  🔭

The Cloth of St Gereon is the oldest known European tapestry still existing, dating to the early 11th century. Parts of it exist in a number of museums.  The tapestry formerly hung in the choir of St Gereon's Church, Cologne.

A series of camels carved into desert rock faces in north-western Saudi Arabia are actually prehistoric, dating from 7,000-8,000 years ago - before either the Pyramids of Giza or Stonehenge were built.

Thamugadi in Algeria was designed to be home to 10,000 retired legionaries, but soon outgrew its original allocation.Because of the remarkable state of preservation of the ruins & the unique example of Roman urban planning with clearly delineated grids, it was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site

For the 17th day of ClassicsTober (Atalanta), a sarcophagus depicting the Calydonian Boar Hunt. Meleager stands at center, and to his right is Atalanta with her bow, drawing an arrow from her quiver. Found in Vicovaro, now in the Musei Capitolini in Rome.

AncientBlueSky 🏺

The Valley of Fires (Carrizozo Volcanic Field) formed only 5,200 years ago when lava spilled out of Little Black Peak and Broken Back Crater (cinder cones/vents) covering the landscape with these black pāhoehoe lava flows. It feels like a combination of Hawaiian terrain with Southwestern flora. 🌿
Sometimes I think about how furry art is older than agriculture. This is the Lion-man. It’s 30 to 40 thousand years old, carved out of mammoth ivory and is the oldest known statue. Period.

My favourite piece of 18th-century bling: the "Oceans Coach", an ornate carriage made at the behest of King John V of Portugal to demonstrate the wealth of the Portuguese empire to Pope Clement XI in Rome in 1716. patrimoniocultural.gov.pt/pt/news/comu...

The Löwenmensch figurine, also called the Lion-man of Hohlenstein-Stadel, is a prehistoric ivory sculpture discovered in Hohlenstein-Stadel, a German cave, in 1939. Determined by carbon dating to be 35,000-41,000 years old, it is one of (if not *the*) oldest anthropomorphic art pieces.

A beautiful socketed axe and a casting mould fragment from Hungary. Socketed axes are between the most widely used tool types of the Late Bronze Age Carpathian Basin.
NHM Vienna #Archaeology🏺
Three Roman mosaic flowers, laid within a mosaic in Rome about 1900 years ago - colourful & beautiful! The mosaic they're part of is now in display at the Palazzo Massimo museum in Rome.

Two golden bowls or ceremonial caps from the Late Bronze Age (1000-850 BC), found in 1972 at Axtroki, in the municipality of Escoriaza, Gipuzkoa, Spain. Nicely displayed at the Museo Arqueológico Nacional, Madrid
🏺 AncientBlueSky

I just love this manuscript. European Columbines and Sweet Cherry, from Mira Calligraphiae Monumenta (a calligraphy manual!), made in Vienna by Georg Bocskay (text, 1562) and Joris Hoefnagel (illumination c. 1591-1596). 
At the Getty Museum, Ms. 20 (86.MV.527), fol. 28.

The world's oldest condom, made of pig intestines in 1640 CE, discovered in Lund, Sweden. The owners manual advised men to dip it in unboiled milk before use to prevent diseases when engaging with prostitutes. It’s washable and reusable. On display at Tirolean County Museum in Austria.

A touch of ancient colour! Discovered in 1834 at the House of the Ancient Hunt, Pompeii (VII.4.48), this panel shows a gorgeously-attired Ariadne handing the skein of thread over to a blue-chlamys-clad Theseus. 

ClassicsBlueSky 

Image: National Archaeological Museum, Naples (9048)

Part of the Valchitran Treasure, a hoard of gold vessels and discs from Bulgaria. Discovered in 1924, its date has been discussed ever since. Opinions based on stylistic comparisons range from the 2nd to the 1st Millennium BCE. Archaeological Museum Sofia. #Archaeology 🏺

The Mosaic of Bacchus, discovered in 2009 in Saint-Laurent-d'Agny near Lyon, is thought to be the oldest known representation of the god of wine on a mosaic in Gaul. It was created around AD 10-14 and decorated the triclinium floor of a Roman domus. Bacchus is crowned with ivy and holding a thyrsus.

This is a marvellous Roman mosaic found at Italica (birthplace of both Trajan and Hadrian IIRC). 

Its obviously very realistic in appearance, but it also seems to seethe with the energy and rage of an angry lion. Love it. 

🕰️C3rd CE
🏛️ Seville Archaeological Museum 
📷 Carole Raddato
🏺 AncientBlueSky

Though not much survives, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus must have been a literally awesome sight. 

Here’s a reconstruction from National Geographic showing the whole city (left) and a closer view from DK. 

I also attach pics of 2 lions from the BM that decorated it (📷 mine)
🏺 AncientBlueSky

The landscapes of central and northern Germany were once full of megalithic graves. Many have been destroyed to produce material for road construction in the 19th century. Lübbensteine, near Helmstedt in Lower Saxony, Germany, ca. 3500 BCE. #Archaeology🏺

Stacked Roman amphora fragments at Monte Testaccio in #Rome, essentially an ancient dumping ground for unwanted vessels (reusing not being a notable phenomenon) - these are just a small number of up to 53 MILLION vessels abandoned here in antiquity!

For MosaicMonday, from the Archaeological Museum of Sparta, a mosaic fragment depicting a rather shifty looking Alcibiades. The 5th century BCE statesman is identified by the mosaicked inscription. Found locally in Sparta and dated to the 1st to 4th century CE.

AncientBlueSky 🏺

In the early Renaissance, it was popular for Europeans to import Islamic artisan goods, like the famous Baptistere de Saint Louis, probably originating from Mamluk Egypt but appearing in France in the late 1300s or early 1400s, signed by the artist Muhammed ibn al-Zayn

The reliquary of the jaw of St. Anthony of Padua (Basilica del Santo, Padua) is crazy enough as it is, but in the modern times they added two light sources, to illuminate it better. The lights reflect from a glass sphere that holds the jaw, looking like ghostly eyes.

(See the 3d photo for no-eyes)

Some lovely Roman glassware. This large turquoise bottle was found at the burial site of an affluent, though not elite, Romano-British couple in Verulanium (now St Albans). Although it’s a relatively simple piece, its survival is incredible & makes it special 
📷 mine 🏺 AncientBlueSky

Belt buckles and bracelets made from Spondylus shells, a species living in the Mediterranean / Black Sea in depths around 15m, were between the favorite ornaments of the Linear Pottery Culture in Central Europe between 5500-4800 BCE. Historisches Museum Regensburg. #Archaeology 🏺

Holy moly! This looks like some glorious Ottoman helmet, but no, it’s Iron Age Celtic. 

This is the Agris Helmet found in France, the work of Gallic craftsmen from c350BCE. An iron dome is coated in fine gold leaf & coral. It’s breathtaking.

With modern digital sensors, you don't want to be shooting in direct sun. The shadows are too harsh and the highlights too bright.

Singleaf piñon, Pinus monophylla, is the only single-needle pine - all others have 2-5 needles in bundles. It has large seeds, piñones, that are delicious. Today's Gardening Advice: If you're looking for a deep red daylily, Buckyballs is an excellent choice.  The flowers are extremely dark and the foliage tends to be evergreen in warmer climates. It's not especially picky about soil (like most daylilies) but does prefer full sun.  🌱

Cardinal Basil! A highly fragrant basil that grows to 24” tall. Bright green leaves contrast large, wine red flower clusters that fade to a dusty plum. Beneficial to pollinators, aroma deters common garden pests. 🌱💚

My 15-year-old jade plant recently went through a rough patch where she looked horrible— shriveled, drooping, discolored. Did you know that your plants’ soil can become hydrophobic? Well, a good repotting took care of that, and now my girl is back to her old self. Much to my relief.

The plant with the blue-green leaves is, surprisingly to me, actually a fern! Coffee fern/coffee cliffbrake. It grows on rocky outcrops in the chaparral and other drier environments, and its leaves change from green to purplish red as they age (fern in the background is a polypody of some sort) 🌿
🌱 Second year growing these dwarf “cosmic orange” sulphur cosmos and they are as fantastic as ever. Incredibly bright orange, floriferous, easy care—can’t ask for a better late-summer annual.

I have been cataloguing my thistles today. This is Carduus nutans, Musk Thistle or Nodding Thistle, a plant of pasture, roadside verges, & other grassy habitats with us in North Yorkshire. Has a fragrance of musk, or almonds. Blooming in August.

I planted this Fuschia in the ground last summer because it got aphids and I just wanted it to live or die. It inexplicably overwintered (zone 6), regrew, and bloomed beautifully. We report: the mimosa trees are blooming bright yellow in the freezing rain. Every year when they bloom, we get surprised - middle of the winter, every other plant is putting its energy into braving the cold, yet the mimosa tree loudly bursts into song. We have the sniffles.

TIL: Haas Avocado trees bloom March - May with each flower lasting only 2 days. The flower opens in the morning as a female, and then the following afternoon as a male. Seems wild and while they self pollinate the best harvests come from cross pollinating. 🌱

“Physics engines are incredibly powerful. Why isn’t it used in World of Warcraft or League of Legends?”

My answer:
* Multiplayer games are incredibly expensive to run
* Physics is expensive to calculate
* Keeping all clients in sync with the combination of the two is  incredibly difficult

You know, it strikes me how live service games 'failing to meet expectations' despite dominating the industry is so weird when you consider that LS games are never permitted to be "Okay." By design, their budgets cannot accept less than "Stellar" and intrinsically some games *must* be just "Okay."

The North American Water Shrew is our smallest diving mammal at only 14-16cm long. It is primarily nocturnal, hunting in the pitch black of rivers and ponds by using its long whiskers to feel and blowing air bubbles which it then inhales to smell for prey.

A corporation is an entity controlled by shareholders that exploits its assets to create maximum benefit for its collective owners.
A union is an entity controlled by its members to exploit their assets (time, intellect, and labor) to create maximum benefit for its collective members.

Malagasy vocabulary:

Laoka: a side dish that’s served with rice.

A “normal” Malagasy meal is supposed to be rice with laoka. Many Malagasy people are willing to accept a meal with very little laoka if necessary, but a meal with not enough rice is simply Not a True Meal.

Lazy porridge recipe!

- 125g salted butter
- 250g oat groats
- 1L water
- 0.75L milk
- 1 tsp salt

1. Fry the oats in butter, salt
2. Pour in water, cook in rice cooker on "brown rice" setting
3. Pour in milk, leave on "keep warm" setting
4. Eat when chewy & delicious (~6hrs)

Tonight I saw St Drogo. It’s low-budget, queer, slow-burn, folk horror. I loved the cinematography, and the interesting critical takes on status & community. I also think there’s a lot going on about the nature of desire, and the diverse ways it’s regulated by religion, money, and social groups.

DEATH MACHINE (1994); endearingly loving tribute to the 80s genre flick, loosing a robotic ALIEN into a BLADE RUNNER-esque megacorp HQ during a DIE HARD-style heist. Brad Dourif delightful as an evil tech nerd incel. Stretches its low budget beautifully across its smoky, steely cyberpunk surface.

Bringing Out The Dead doesn't get its due, both as a Scorsese film and as a film capturing the spirit of the late 90s, with possibly Nicholas Cage's best performance. 

It's surprisingly gothic in atmosphere and manages to capture Scorsese's twin passions of New York grime and human spirituality.

the amazing mr x is a twisty, highly-atmospheric horror/thriller from eagle-lion films about a phony spiritualist. it’s pretty great… pretty low budget but the photography is beautiful and the script is tight and clever. shades of the uninvited and nightmare alley….this one is legit. check it out. 📽️

MOSS ROSE is deeply, deliciously weird. Love the absurd logic of Cockney chorus girl Peggy Cummins blackmailing Victor Mature and compelling him to take her to his country estate so that she can learn to be a lady.  Love even more that we are supposed to root for her and want her scheme to succeed.

hey draculas.  today’s rec is CANDYMAN (1992).  a supernatural slasher/haunted house that is very CHICAGO.  it explores the legacy of racism, systematic and interpersonal, past and contemporary in a really sophisticated way through horror.  also not a funny one this time.  and TONY TODD is the lead

Watching a V-Cinema action movie shot in New York, marquee spottings so far: The Return of Superfly, Marked for Death, Death Warrant, Tune in Tomorrow…, Jacob’s Ladder, Savini’s Night of the Living Dead remake, Prince’s Graffiti Bridge, Rocky V, and King of New York

Astaire and Rogers in Top Hat. One of the most platonically perfect movies I’ve ever seen. The dancing is at the  ‘impossible’ level of difficulty. One is reminded of watching Bruce Lee. That these two should also be great at screwball comedy boggles the mind.

Just rewatched Week-End in Havana (1941), which is getting to be one of my comfort movies. It’s one of my favorite Fox musicals… the songs aren’t too good (except for the 3 Carmen Miranda numbers), but it’s a wonderful screwball comedy. All the characters are great and the Technicolor is magnificent

Uncle Peckerhead is one of the best, most heartfelt / punk horror comedies in years, with really great original music, and i feel like a lot of people didn't give it a chance because it has an odd name. You should watch it!

watch Ravenous (1999) for a film that combines a sharp critique of manifest destiny, a suggestion that cannibalism somehow gives you super powers, deep homoeroticism and one of the wildest tones you've ever seen - all in one really weird movie

The Thing. 1982. dir: John Carpenter

There’s a LOT to like about this film: the ensemble cast, Carpenter’s direction, Ennio Morricone’s score, Rob Bottin’s astounding physical effects work, the tense paranoia among the crew, and Dean Cundey’s exceptional cinematography.

Serie Noire (1979)

A superb, bleakly hilarious film noir about a door-to-door salesman who is lured into crime by a teenage prostitute.  Based on the Jim Thompson novel A Hell of a Woman.  

Directed by Alain Corneau

Screenplay by Corneau and Georges Perec, who was BOTD in 1936

A few years ago, I came upon an excellent and suspenseful British hidden gem called THE APPPOINTMENT (1982). There was no hope for a re-release back then, but BFI did the impossible. Wrote some words about the film at Bloody Disgusting.

Didn't know what to expect from Doctor X (1932) but I was not prepared for a movie this luscious, creepy and funny. A two-toned marvel full of gloomy Gothic settings and Art Deco mad science in stunning, sickly Technicolor. A blast from Michael Curtiz (Casablanca!) in one of his rare horror forays.
Poor Things is enchantingly weird, existential, even hilarious. A visual feast, and a fucking delight. Brilliant! I loved it 🖤

A shockingly violent film, but also a very stylish/thrilling one. I won't even begin to pretend that this flick is in anything but bad taste.  But bad taste is what fans of a film like this want, and Takashi Harada grasps how far he can push the limits without descending into out and out vileness.

THEY CLONED TYRONE - provocative, satirical sci-fi with an exceptional cast that blends Blaxploitation and absurdist humor. Wildly entertaining and dripping with style and social commentary. A mix of THEY LIVE, GROUNDHOG'S DAY, and US. Boyega, Foxx, and Parris are FANTASTIC.

Fifty years today, arguably Ray Harryhausen’s magnum opus, and certainly one of my seminal texts, received its London release. A truly astonishing cast, a hugely evocative Miklós Rózsa score, an inventive screenplay, and some of cinema’s most monstrously beautiful creatures!

PARIS IS BURNING (1990)
Dir. Jennie Livingston
United States
Documentary, Queer
#DesertIslandSundance

Where does voguing come from, and what is throwing shade? This landmark documentary provides a vibrant snapshot of the 80s through the eyes of New York's Black and Latine Harlem drag-ball scene.

Just finished View to a Kill on the Bond rewatch. Not an objectively good Bond but so much fun after the chore of Octopussy. Roger Moore’s old man noises dubbed onto his stunt doubles are unintentionally hilarious. Walken & Jones having chemistry. Patrick Macnee there to make Moore seem younger.

Revisited Lake Placid (1999) this evening. Hot damn, that is a very 90’s movie. The dialogue belongs in a 90’s museum. Bill Pullman gives absolutely nothing to his role. But the CGI holds up surprisingly well, the crocodile still looks great! And of course very large. 🐊

Just watched Cry of the City (1948), a terrific noir film with Richard Conte as an escaped murderer trying to escape the city. Fast paced, hard dialogue, and exceedingly good performances by Conte and Victor Mature. Highly recommended for noir aficionados.

Palm Springs (2020) really impressed me. It's not the greatest film ever, but it is one of those rare movies that quickly established its tone and expectations before accomplishing exactly what it set out to accomplish in a tight 90 minutes. Plus, it was fun! 📽️

A film that’s haunted me since it’s release in 1990 is Jacob's Ladder. Vietnam vet Tim Robbins sees demons wherever he goes & has no idea why. The film's all practical special effects have had an outsized impact on pop culture, influencing everything from other movies to video games, eg Silent Hill

Watched a couple different rom-coms last night, My Best Girl from 1927 and No Hard Feelings from 2023. The formula  stays the same over a century — two mismatched people come together over a lie, they have some crazy fun, they fall for each other, the lie is revealed, but they get a happy ending.

Another one I love so very much that, like Ravenous, has finally started to get the love and attention it so richly deserves is Pontypool. It's such an odd little film. Shot almost entirely in a single location, with much if not all of the action taking place outside, offscreen. But it is so *TENSE*

"Talk To Me" on Netflix is a cracking little horror movie. I went into it thinking it was going to be the usual thing - bunch of pretty American teenagers running and screaming. It's Australian and SO much better than that. Actually pretty scary. Loved the ending.

SALTBURN. Starts as A SEPARATE PEACE, becomes THE GREAT GATSBY meets CALL ME BY MY NAME, then becomes something so dark and sinister it’s very much its own thing. Sharply hilarious and pitch black to the core. Critics will not be able to stop talking about this all awards season. LOVED IT.

THE EXORCIST hasn’t lost a shred of the sheer power it held over me as a kid. Horrific, vicious animal of a horror film that claws and bites at the soul. Will never lose its place as one of if not THE scariest films ever made

26/31

MARTIN (1977) is the strangest film of Romero's storied career. Of all the damn things, I'm reminded of MEMENTO, with an unreliable narrator explaining how the vampire world works over the phone to an unseen voice while mysteries unfold in a mix of b&w and color. One of my fav vampire films.

Watched Švankmajer's FAUST (1994) again. Probably my favourite of his Surrealist delights. Rabbit hole layers of wonderful strangeness and endless tactile invention. The lifesize puppets trotting around are never not very funny. One of the best screen devils. Proper magic of cinema, baby...

A recommendation! Mario Bava's BLACK SABBATH (1963)!

Bava tackles the horror anthology, delivering three technicolor nightmares of steadily increasing TERROR. You get Boris Karloff as a cryptkeeper style host / a terrifying vampire, as well as one of the scariest segments ever in A Drop Of Water.

A strong recommendation for 'Poker Face', Rian 'Knives Out' Johnson's TV series which partially answers that question about whether Natasha Lyonne would make a good Columbo. Each episode is a compact movie and episode 9, 'Escape from Shit Mountain', is especially cinematic. Not bleak! Not grey! 📺📽

MONTGOMERY CLIFT watching his own performance in the 1949 film “The Heiress”.

Taken by Life photographer J.R. Eyerman these strangely intimate images capture the star shifting around in his seat apprehensively watching the screen almost scared of what he’s seeing.

📽️

The Matrix and John Wick are both Keanu Reeves action movies with no explicit supernatural elements yet I would recommend both of them as required viewing for the World of Darkness - Mage and Vampire respectively

We just watched The Full Monty. Damn, does that movie ever hold up! Men (of the industrial persuasion) being supportive of each other. Discussion about body positivity.
A queer relationship that is accepted as just ... Business as usual.
Truly incredible, 1997.
It's not super kind to Sheffield tho.

Aside from the other benefits of a really good and tight monster movie script, one of the strengths of TREMORS (1990) is that it is a remarkably accurate portrayal of several Types Of Rural Guy in that era, doubtlessly contributing to it standing the test of time as a cinema experience.

Still thinking about last night’s viewing, THE LEGEND OF HELL HOUSE (1973). Loved it. For me it worked as an occult heist film: putting together the crew, scoping out the job, dealing with tensions in the gang etc. Apparently the Richard Matheson source novel goes harder, going to have to read it

The Gorgon (1964)

Starring Peter Cushing, Christopher Lee, and Barbara Shelley

Putting this here in the hidden opinion vault: Authentic cut of Twixt is my favorite Coppola film. Feels like someone reversed the wiring on a guy maddin homage to PS2 survival horror cut scenes, seems like it should be nothing but archness but it is blisteringly, painfully earnest. Just incredible.

United States, Sweden
Horror, Drama, Cult

A grieving woman accompanies her boyfriend and his grad-school colleagues to a remote Swedish village's fabled mid-summer festival, only to discover that the idyllic commune isn't what it appears to be.

Ed Lachman’s cinematography for EL CONDE is mesmerizing: its exquisite, uncanny abstractions of shadow and light are the film’s main artistic triumph, at times genuinely evocative of Dreyer and Murnau in its visual and spiritual depth. Sumptuous, awe-striking work.

Demon Queen (1987, Donald Farmer). Hypnotic, near-plotless SOV full of wicked vibes and droney synthscapes. Incredible banger soundtrack by Jan Haflin that sounds like Patrick Cowley (in both his italo/NRG and porn soundtrack modes). 50 minutes of magic. Hell yeah hell yeah

My god, Cronenberg's THE FLY is so profoundly sad. It could've been a cheap shocker, but Jeff Goldblum portrays a character that we *genuinely* care for. If you've ever had a loved one with a degenerative disease, this hits like a sledgehammer.

A recent online poll judged Monty Python's Holy Grail to be the best film of the 70s. Considering that decade gave us the first two Godfathers, Jaws, Star Wars, Dog Day Afternoon, and Chinatown (to name but a few), I'm not persuaded we have 20/20 hindsight yet. Even Rocky Horror holds up better.

Quentin Dupieux’s Smoking Causes Coughing gave me some of my hardest laughs of the year. Deeply silly, kinda lovely, best environmental message movie this year. Power Rangers via Tales From the Crypt. Great stuff.

Thinking about The Archers (as every film buff does) I just realized that THE RED SHOES and BLACK NARCISSUS are fundamentally horror films that happen to be family-friendly. Especially BLACK NARCISSUS. What a weird, astonishing Technicolour nightmare!

Rewatched Peter Weir’s MASTER AND COMMANDER: THE FAR SIDE OF THE WORLD on the big screen in 35mm at Karlovy Vary International Film Festival and I came so near to weeping for the kind of epic cinema we’re never gonna get again. A masterpiece.

Rewatched GLENGARRY GLEN ROSS last night. It’s a truly a prime example of how you can drop an audience in the middle of something, give them almost no exposition, and not only will they figure things out—but it will be damn compelling.

I will die on the hill that 1988's remake of The Blob is as amazing and important as Carpenter's The Thing when it comes to its practical effects. The garbage disposal guy? The PHONE BOOTH DEATH?? Ugh, it's so good. Plus, the lesser Dillon and his glorious mullet.

Breaking news in two things can be true: IT FOLLOWS is a brilliant, formally ingenious horror movie that absolutely did not cry out for a sequel; and I will be first in line to see what David Robert Mitchell does with a second shot at the premise.

22. BROTHERHOOD OF THE WOLF (2001) A dizzying mélange of genres—kung fu, romantic period piece, horror—and themes—reason vs superstition, anti and also pro papal/monarchy/colonialism—induces whiplash. Also, one of the most mindboggling dissolves in history.

Richard Jenkins - 📽️ Flirting with Disaster (David O. Russell, 1996)

Jenkins is such a riot in this road trip comedy. He and Josh Brolin play ATF agents and squabbling lovers who pursue Ben Stiller across the United States. At one point he ingests acid and is hysterical without overplaying anything.

There are two types of hetero relationships: one where Jimmy Stewart succumbs to a paranoid delusion and (maybe) pushes Kim Novak off a bell tower a la Vertigo (1958), the other is Kim Novak giving up witchcraft to be with Jimmy Stewart as seen in Bell, Book and Candle (1958).

Daisy Doodad's Dial (1914)

A silent comedy short about a face-pulling contest.  Florence Turner, who directed and stars, puts on a tour de force exhibition of facial contorting.  Turner was BOTD in 1885.  She's historically noteworthy as one of the first movie stars.

It was understandably overshadowed last weekend but I just saw Cobweb and thought it ruled. Super atmospheric, looks great, genuinely kinda scary and has a goofy Malignant-like sensibility to it. Really fun movie.

The Florida Project (2017) This accurately delves into the lives of people who live in motels long term. Excellent storytelling. Brooklynn & Bria were so transcendent you’d think they were actually mother & daughter. 2 hours of well saturated Floridian landscape & hard reality. Stunning. #filmsky

Alone in the Dark (1982)

A stone cold early 80s horror classic.  Not unlike The Dream Team (1989) if Michael Keaton and co. were all homicidal maniacs who wanted to kill their doctor.

Directed by Jack Sholder

Starring Martin Landau, Donald Pleasence, and Jack Palance, who was BOTD in 1919

Rewatch Evil Dead II and then marvel at the brilliance of Raimi’s direction and Campbell’s physical comedy. What makes the movie so sublime is its arch sense of self-awareness — rooted entirely in a focus on the interior. Wrote a whole article about it last year in @@19757:

JOHNNY GUNMAN heavily borrows its melodrama from 50s’ juvenile delinquency films, giving this one-night-in-NYC gangster noir a distinctive attitude of romantic nihilism. A low budget & raw performances add rather than detract from its air of authenticity: Art Ford shoulda made more! #Noirvember

learning that Konaka wrote Evil Dead Trap 2 is v. unsurprising, "what if the lain guy wrote a giallo" is the films whole deal. televised grotesquerie, memetic paranoia, predatory cults, the lurking industrial under the sheen of the misogynist capitalist neon-soaked no-future- *the* Lost Decade movie

Clive Owen - 📽️ Croupier (Mike Hodges, 1999)

A star is born in this one, where Owen takes the lead as a real fuckin’ cool casino croupier and aspiring author caught in a suave noirish crime web. I’m a huge Owen fan, and here he’s one of the few people who makes me love narration in modern film.

I WAKE UP SCREAMING (1941)

No one actually wakes up screaming but otherwise this is a top notch noir about the murder of an actress.  

Directed by H. Bruce Humberstone

Starring Victor Mature, Laird Cregar (one of the great actor's best performances), and Betty Grable, who was BOTD in 1916.

THE BICYCLE THIEF (1948)
Dir. Vittorio De Sica
Italy
Drama

Unemployed Antonio is elated when he finally finds work hanging posters around war-torn Rome. However on his first day, his bicycle — essential to his work — gets stolen. His job is doomed unless he can find the thief.

I hadn’t known Peter Gabriel did the score for THE LAST TEMPTATION OF CHRIST. Scorsese & Schrader craft an interesting rumination on the internal, eternal push-pull between man’s wants & his spiritual needs/ calling. Willem Dafoe gives a incredibly compelling performance.

This will sound like a joke but it’s not: the Milli Vanilli documentary is absolutely fucking riveting. 

Having lived through that era I knew most of the details of the story, but the film is an amazing deep-dive into what seemed like little more than a punchline at the time. Highly recommended.

Last night's watch, the Criterion Collection's restored  ISLAND OF LOST SOULS (1932). I've only seen the butchered, sanitized version that was on tv. 

HG Wells hated it, but it's a disturbing film, and Charles Laughton is magnificent as the malevolent Dr. Moreau.

James Mason - 📽️ Odd Man Out (Carol Reed, 1947)

Noir setups don’t get much leaner than watching Mason as an IRA man hiding from police, but the Belfast setting and Reed’s English sensibilities make it distinct from the American stuff. Mason is one of the all-timers, and this is close to his best.

Just watched The Sky’s the Limit (1943), loved it. Kind of a trifle, plot wise, but Fred gets to do some dramatic acting, and he does it well. Joan Leslie is fine but this is almost like a solo Astaire movie. The scene where he’s drunk and dancing through a bar destroying things is just marvelous.

n(r)w: “The Haunting” (1963)

Something to fold clothes to. IMO this flick is one of the all-time horror films. Its lushness B&W framing, its use of sound, its psychosexual underpinnings. Robert Wise putting to use everything he learned at RKO, working off arguably the best of all horror novels.

Ida Lupino was impressed enough by Peggy Dow’s work in “Woman in Hiding” that she tried to get Dow on loan out to star in her production, “Outrage” (1950). Universal-International and Howard Hughes couldn’t agree on terms and Lupino eventually cast Mala Powers.

Saw Poor Things, which is either a radical masterpiece or an offensive trainwreck, and I'll be able to decide which in about five years.

How can you not smile after something like Roger Corman’s A BUCKET OF BLOOD? Dick Miller plays a timid busboy whose thriving art career is born of murder. Deviously funny sense of humor. Julian Burton is captivating as the esteemed art snob.

Since you’re enjoying the red-winged blackbird pic (& name), here are some tricolored blackbirds. Diff species. Found mostly in CA. Grassland specialists. Endangered.

Similar to red-winged, but males have white wing patch (not orange/yellow) and females are darker with clearer eyebrow stripe.

#BirdGlamour’s Halloween-colored birds continues with Black-vented Orioles! These blackbird relatives call Central & South America home but are occasionally spotted in AZ & TX. Black-vented Orioles love an open area with scattered trees. Their name comes from their black vent (aka bum) area. 🐡🧪

The kingfisher that lives by my place finally agreed to let me photograph her! Just after this she caught a fish nearly a third her size and proceeded to whack it against the branch until it was dead.

Belted Kingfisher - San Francisco, CA 🪶
Doesn’t get much more magnificent than Trumpeter swans in Oregon’s desert country. These amazing birds against these rugged landscapes are just beautiful.

Many think of Marbled Godwits as prairie birds (well coastal in winter) but there are also breeding populations on the James Bay lowlands and on the Alaska Peninsula. This one is from the #Alaska population during a stopover on the Anchor River State Recreation Area 🪶

Bird Glamour’s Glamager series continues with Hepatic Tanagers! This southern US to Central American dark red bird loves a pine-oak forest. These birds are little studied, but we do know they eat insects, spiders, and small fruits. Lady Hepatic Tanagers do most of the nest building. 🐡

Welcome to the #BirdGlamour Glamager series, starting with the Western Tanager from western North America! The Western Tanager is extra and DOES NOT get his red coloration from a diet rich in carotenoids like many birds do: their red comes from rhodoxanthin from their insect-rich diet. 🐡🐦

I learned on Saturday that California has its own race of Red-winged Blackbird that has no yellow in its shoulder patch - the California Bicolored Blackbird.

I gotta admit: these birds were stunners. It’s amazing what a little color difference can do.

god i love watching a reddish egret just launch itself through the water, wings out, head swinging to and fro. It's a hilarious method of hunting AND IT WORKS. these dudes rustle up a ton of food running around like a maniac in the water.

Great egrets: masters of the art of striking a pose. With a slow, sassy strut, they wade through the waters in pursuit of their aquatic prey. Showcasing their prowess as ambush predators, these birds are striking in more than one way! Nature’s choreography unfolds in these feathered maestros.

Best bird photos from 2023.
When word got out that rare scarlet-chested parrots had been seen in big numbers at Gluepot, birders (including me) flocked to see them. I had searched for these birds for years. This is a female scarlet-chested parrot feeding on cottony saltbush.
🪶 #birds

Bird of the day.. Waxwing (Bombycilla garrulus) We’ve had quite the irruption of these bandit masked bounty hunters this year! Our locale is blessed with juniper, rowan & mistletoe berries. They now move on to orchards new.. a joy all told these past few weeks..🪶

A Montane Woodcreeper working on a tasty moth. The bird is bashing the moth on the tree to knock off the scales on the moth's wings. These birds hitch up trees like woodpeckers while foraging for insects. 🪶🌿🧪

A stunning Scarlet-Bellied Mountain Tanager working on some feather care - the bird was happily bathing. These fruit eating birds can be found in the high forests of the Andes Mountains from Venezuela to Bolivia. 🌿🧪🪶🐡
Zuroloma Birding, Nono, Ecuador
A great blue heron about to devour a crayfish.  Taken just a few days ago, 3-Oct-2023 in Sterling, Virginia, USA.

These birds are absolute rock stars and I am beyond thrilled to have seen them at last! 😍#BirdPhotography #NaturePhotography #WildlifePhotography 🌿

I hear it's Black-crowned night heron day. Count me in. They're such sleek birds. Found on every continent except Australia and Antarctica, they are the most widespread heron species in the world! #Birds

When birding in your own garden in South Africa gets interesting. A pair of African Hoopoes successfully raised a Greater Honeyguide.

This morning on the Boston side of the river, by Mass Ave and Storrow, I saw a young female bald eagle swoop into the Charles and then a second later it was flying over me with a fish in its talons. Various waterbirds, taken from a great distance during our yurt stay last week: red-necked grebe, common loon, red-breasted mergansers. All perfectly at home on the aptly-named Bird Lake in Manitoba.

This half-ounce blackpoll warbler undertakes an epic migration journey - from the boreal forest north of here to spend winter in South America. It didn't stay long in my garden 🪶

One of the easiest, best things we've ever done for your yard is just deciding to let most of it be. We had a slim dead tree that fell towards the back last year, and this log has been a focal point for all kinds of wildlife, including this male Pileated Woodpecker this morning. 🪶

Superb Lyrebird outside my window! There were actually two of them, but the other one was a little further back in the bushes. Here’s a 10-second video of it having a scratch. drive.google.com/file/d/1QIsc...
iconic Australian landscape - superb parrots at their nest hollow in an old red gum, with kangaroos grazing in the shade

Good to see the resident pied oystercatchers at Bald Hill Beach working on their family planning. They have been so unlucky. Every year they try. Every year they fail to become parents. Maybe this time?

Sunday afternoon went birding with a friend in South Louisiana. As the sun was setting we noticed a large amount of Scissor-tailed Flycatchers. A careful 1x1 count and got us 53! As we were leaving they started to roost in the Oak trees. Quite a sight just an hour south of New Orleans!
Warbler migration is ramping up. Fall warblers can be hard to identify, but thankfully black-and-white warblers are always recognizable. 🪶

Our Halloween-colored #BirdGlamour celebration continues with the Hooded Oriole! Seen in southwest US and Mexico, they’re also known as palm leaf orioles because the sew their sack nests on the undersides of palm fronds. Hooded Orioles are chatterboxes and will mimic woodpeckers and flycatchers!🧪🐡🐦

Tahiti petrel, wheeling over the Coral Sea. These are pelagic birds, rarely seen near land but abundant in certain parts of the Pacific Ocean.

Spatiotemporal abundance of the whitespotted eagle ray and the giant manta ray (Chondrichthyes: Myliobatiformes) from aerial surveys in southeast Florida. 🦑🐟🌎🧪 link.springer.com/article/10.1...

Superb owl photo my wife took in 2016 in Brian Piccolo Park near Fort Lauderdale. The park is full of nesting burrowing owls who have no problem living among the people using the park for recreation, it’s really an amazing thing to see.

This palm warbler was one of a pair I saw zipping along near ground level, gleaning food. They eat primarily insects but will also eat seeds and berries. They also nest on the ground. Very un-warblery warbler! 🪶

🪶 A few white-faced storm-petrels have been seen at Altona this past fortnight. This migratory seabird has a global range and doesn't make its way into the bay very often. After three trips, I finally got this pic with about ten minutes of light left in the day.
Male hooded oriole. They are here in SoCal from about March through August for the most part & are usually found and heard around skirted palm trees.

Willow ptarmigan are such fun birds. Like many northern species, they moult into a nearly all-white plumage for winter to blend into their surroundings. However, they still stick out a bit when standing on crushed ice. 🪶🌿

A bar-tailed godwit developing its breeding plumage ahead of its big flight soon.
We don't often see this colouring in Australia. They fly way up north of the Arctic Circle to breed each year.
These birds hold the world record for non-stop flight.

we get lots of raptors around our house, and although i generally don't care too much about bald eagles, i appreciate that they're a bird i can't mistake for anything else. there's no Davidson's Pale-Headed Megafalcon out there to trip me up when i'm trying to teach the kids what's flying overhead

Various Sandhill Crane head shots at the lakefront.

Male straight at ya, then three shots of the female. The last pic of the back of the head shows two gray feather bumps one on each side, those are the cranes ears.

Ruby Throated Hummingbird migration still passing through the Florida Panhandle. Most of the males are long gone by now, but I'm still seeing the females, like this beautiful girl backlit by the morning sun.

The Bald Eagles at the local park will sometimes take sticks from the Great Blue Heron rookery and add them to their nest. This Bald Eagle picked up a stick, but the stick must not have met the Eagle's quality standards because it was dropped a few moments after this photo was taken.

We love this funky, punky Goldcrest, shared with our Nature Table group by Moi Hicks.
Weighing in at less than 6 grams, the Goldcrest is UK's smallest bird (along with the less common Firecrest).

It was unrelentingly grey, rainy and bitterly cold here all weekend but I was glad to have ventured out to Beddington Farmlands in south London when this handsome little Eurasian Kestrel landed in a tree about ten metres from me and decided to hang out. 🪶

Sungrebe (Heliornis fulica) at Caño Negro Wildlife Refuge.

American White Ibis working its way across a flooded field looking for lunch. I took this at Sheldon Lake state park.
Surfbirds at Alki Beach Christmas Eve. Surfbirds are small wading shore birds that nest on the Alaska tundra but overwinter on the Pacific Northwest coast: 🪶

The power of camouflage - black-faced sand grouse in Tarangire National Park, Tanzania.

Townsend's solitaire at a cemetery in Denver 🪶

It's the only "solitaire" native to the US, which are more closely related to bluebirds than other regional thrushes in Turdidae, like the robins or the Catharus "nightingale-thrushes".
🪶 Song sparrow eating a grasshopper and perching in a black-eyed Susan. Montrose Bird Sanctuary, Chicago, today. Could be wrong about bird and plant ID (but pretty sure about date and location!).

Great Blue Herons are typically solitary birds when out fishing. Very unusual to see two, let alone three or more, together, outside of a heron rookery. These three were part of a group of six herons fishing Alki Beach last summer: 🪶

Little Egret in Bishop's Stortford. Could be better, but nice to finally get a photo of my local patch bogey bird. Seen them on occasion but they are so skittish around here they usually take flight before I'm in range. Hopefully they get more used to the people and dog traffic along the Stort.

Spotted a reef heron at the beach twice now.  nzbirdsonline.org.nz/species/reef... "A bird of the rocky shore. It can also be seen on estuary mudflats and occasionally wading at sandy beaches. The population is estimated at only 300-500, but appears stable. Usually solitary."

When it's 15° F / -9.4° C out, an uneasy détente develops around the suet. The Downy Woodpecker, despite being the smallest woodpecker on the continent, is still an insane jackhammer dinosaur, and generally everyone keeps their distance. This Bluebird decided to roll the dice. Tense. 🪶 #bird

Celebrated the holiday by forcing my long-suffering father to search for hours for Red-cockaded Woodpeckers

Brown creeper photo would make a devilish jigsaw puzzle! These tiny birds stick close to the trunks of large loose-barked trees, probing for insects. The start at the bottom and work their way up, then move to the base of the next one 🪶

I’ve had few opportunities to get out this month but managed a quick visit to Rodley Nature Reserve in Leeds this morning. Grey and windy. 37 species, including goosander, grey wagtail, sparrowhawk, kingfisher. Enjoyable semi-urban #birding!

Planning your own "fall migration" for some leaf peeping? 🍂 Your journey probably won't take you as far as our Bird of the Week! Swainson's Hawks have the longest migration of any North American raptor. Learn about ABC's role in their recovery at bit.ly/3RvZURZ. 🪶

Today started with very cold temperatures, I got to see some surprise visitors - Pine Siskins, whom I only see here every other odd year. They are goldfinch size, have pointy beaks, Goldfinch temperament and some yellow on the wings. Feisty little buggers.

And these photos I took many years ago in November in Ternopil. It's not black&white photos. It's just that day was very grey and with dark monotonous sky. And countless ravens were sitting on the trees in the park. And then suddenly they started to fly simultaneously. Part 1.

Red-necked stints (like these at Bald Hill Beach) are our smallest migratory shorebirds.

This wedge-tailed eagle (different nest from the one I showed earlier) took me by surprise. I was wandering around Bundera Dam at Boolcoomatta looking for the crimson chats I had seen there the day before ... then looked up to see mama wedgie looking at me! This shows the scale of their nests. 🪶

We have a local barred owl pair that nests along the Salado Creek every year. While they were still in the area this year, they must’ve moved the location of the nest. They were bothered by a lot of curious folks last year and only one chick made it. I’m always happy to see them around though.

Dead chuffed the Bohemian Waxwings stuck around in Balham until I got back to London! It's turning out to be a great "waxwing winter" in the UK - so happy to have had the chance to see these gorgeous Scandinavian irruptive visitors feasting on berries just a 15 minute bike ride from home. 🪶
A Red-winged Blackbird fledgling sits in the grass, listening to Mom's constant contact calls - she is quite an acrobat as she hunts for bugs - a fledgling in the tree is fed 🪶🌿

My friend Barry, the Bare-throated Tiger-Heron at Tapir Valley Nature Reserve, Costa Rica. I was lucky to be able to spend many hours with this young bird as it learned to hunt along the edge of the canals.

#birds #herons 🪶

Dad and Mom Mallard taking a relaxing swim while the little ones are safely resting on lily pads. Third in a series, that did not start out as a series. 🙂 My recollection is that either an Egret or Canada Goose was nearby and Dad was trying to scare them off. Lagoon, SF Bay.

Went for a little wander around Leverett Pond yesterday and saw this slightly odd duck. Someone at iNaturalist tells me the bill coloration is probably the result of poor nutrition, not hybridization or anything like that? #birds 🪶

My favourite gull is the Great black-backed gull (not 'Greater black-back' as often named), which I'm pleased to say is often seen around the coasts here (southern England). It can reach 78 cm in length, weigh 2 kg, and have a wingspan of 1.65 m. The one here (from Weymouth) has a dirty throat.

#BirdGlamour celebrates the Altamira Oriole! This tropical oriole lives year-round in Mexico & Central America and they JUST makes it into southern TX/Rio Grande.  Females weave elaborate hanging nests up to 26 inches long. They love insects & forage dead grasshoppers off of the fronts of cars!🐡🧪🐦

White tern perched in an ironwood (Causuarina equisetifolia) tree, where the species "nests"... except they construct no nest to speak of! They precariously balance a bare egg within the ironwood's branches.

Photo from Saipan, CNMI 🪶

Yikes! A bald eagle is a rare sight in this area, but I caught one passing way overhead (P1). Zooming P1 shows it better, if blurry. But then he circled to fly directly over (P3), and as a zoom on P4 shows, looked right at me. 🦅 📸📷

Last week I got to watch a particularly striking Song Sparrow foraging in the fallen leaves and berries of a California Pepper Tree - I managed to get a shot just before it chomped down on this rolled up isopod 🪶

Just finished @@346220 's MAD SISTERS OF ESI and it's magnificent, a tale of tales wrapped in iridescent spacetime, an infinitely nested creation myth, a portal and a ship and a campfire woven of prose. Reminded me of Calvino, and Clarke's PIRANESI (but spacefaring).

This really is a roller coaster of a read. What at first appears to be a light-hearted tale of 1930s bohemian London goes on to encompass illness, destitution and tragic loss, but still finds room for comedy. A gem of a novel. My first by Barbara Comyns but not my last.
Please read Dark Harvest by Norman Partridge, which is a lot like if Ray Bradbury wrote a small-town supernatural slasher.

In one of my audiobook groups someone asked for “weirdest/grossest/most disturbing” horror novels. Some people are suggesting Dean Koontz and James Patterson. I mean, I guess experiences may vary. I just sent them a link to @@62103’s Splattepunk awards.

Just finished Lucifer by Dan Watters, Max Fiumara, Sebastian Fiumara et al. 

Couldn’t hit my sweet spot more if it tried. Gorgeous art, great story and definitely a strong compliment to the wider Sandman world.

If you see this, post a book you’ve read more than once.

Spare, bleak, and brutal, WE WHO ARE ABOUT TO… demolishes many of the village pieties of genre SF. It’s also very funny. 

It was originally published in GALAXY during the editorship of Jim Baen. Which is to say, people are complicated.

No Shelter But The Stars by Virginia Black, for a story that primarily takes place on a barren rock or in space, this novel is so viscerally lush with emotional depth! Even the most spartan passages hit so that you feel it with your whole chest. Just a hugely satisfying read.

Sapphic books | WLW

Found a wonderful architecture bookstore in Amsterdam, simply called Architectura & Natural Boeken. The urban planning books were completely different than what you’d seen in an American bookstore. It’s like we’re having a completely different conversation than the rest of the world.

MAEVE FLY is dark, perverse, and incredibly violent. It’s a new era of AMERICAN PSYCHO with a gut punch ending. There are secrets lurking in the basement, and they are drenched in blood. It all comes together with the perfect climax that you don’t see coming until it’s too late. I loved this book.🕸️📚

I've heard many books described as "something meets Twin Peaks." James Kennedy's Bride of the Tornado is the first book I've read that lives up to that description. I'm about halfway through and it's so weird and unsettling and a little funny and romantic, and I'm loving it.

The Saint of Bright Doors reads like a novel-length short story in the best way possible: full of fresh ideas, fast-moving, with an evident care applied to each and every sentence. Remarkable and highly-recommended.

Finished Solenoid by Mircea Cartarescu, tr Sean Cotter. A battle at times, but worth the effort I think. A richly imaginative stream/waterslide of consciousness slipping between dream states and reality for a nobody Romanian school teacher. Lots of great lines and tough paragraphs.

Finished Farthings by Charles Boyle – 113 short pieces (a para each) about life as a one man publishing house CBEditions. I enjoyed it enormously. Like Alan Bennett's diaries only with a sharper edge. Miraculously free of industry bitterness, but lots of wry insights about how publishing works.

I have finished reading the latest @@4966 book, What Feasts at Night, and can tell you that the author is one of the best writers of the experience of having a nightmare that I have ever read. Just, captures the fuckin' WEIRDNESS of bad dreams.

A++ 
10/10

i read 3 james m cain novels last night bc i couldn't sleep and i tell ya the famousest ones (double indemnity, the postman always rings twice) are way less good than mildred pierce, which is Very Very Very Good Indeed

Announcing the winner of the 2023 Cercador Prize: @@241041’s translation of Ana Paula Maia's OF CATTLE AND MEN.

The Cercador committee says OF CATTLE AND MEN "lays bare the brutal labor of the slaughterhouse trade," hailing the novel as a "new breed of western."

Incredible little work, this - like Ford’s WELL-BUILT CITY by way of WE HAVE ALWAYS LIVED IN THE CASTLE. One of the most effectively moving finales I’ve ever read. Remarkably consonant with MOTHTOWN. What a time to be alive and reading books about death.

I’ve been reading Discworld for the first time this year and I cannot overstate how good it is. It’s funny, smart, and has just layers of “oh that’s a good point…” that makes you think and hopefully grow.

I wish I had read them sooner.

Absolutely blown away by C. J. Leede's MAEVE FLY, which sets itself higher and higher hurdles and then backflips over every one of them. It invites so many comparisons veteran authors would quake at, but it earns them. Mean, nasty, solipsistic, amazing.

The Case of Cem by Bulgarian writer Vera Mutafchieva deserves to be part of the 20th century canon of global literature. Now, thanks to International Booker winner Angela Rodel, Anglophone readers can discover this epic novel. These are finished copies. Let me know if you want an ARC.

Just finished Malcolm Lowry’s first novel, Ultramarine. A bit purple, and fascinating regarding how much a writer insists on getting out of the “will he cheat on his lady back home question” and whether or not he will get in a fight with the ship’s resident tough dude. Not a bad intro to Lowry.
if you like heists and crooks who aren’t very good at being crooks, i’m begging you to read donald e. westlake’s Dortmunder novels

Amal El-Mohtar is wonderfully generous to THE SAINT OF BRIGHT DOORS in the New York Times: “the best book I’ve read all year. Protean, singular, original … I can’t remember the last time a book made me so excited about its existence, its casual challenge to what a fantasy novel could be.”

Really enjoying Witches Abroad so far. Love how the witches play off of each other, and also love what the story does with fairy tales. Actually wonder if Shrek took any inspiration from it. Also very much feels like Pterry visited New Orleans once and was like. Ah yes. I know this place. Uh. GUMBO

Finished The Sarah Book by Scott McClanahan. An unpasteurised study of the feral grief of relationship & personal breakdown. Simultaneously one of the funniest & saddest books I have ever read. One of the best too. I'm used to book sadness, book poignancy, book emotions – but this is the real thing.

Today's book rec is Paul Beatty's THE SELLOUT, which possesses in great measure what all powerful satires possess: beneath its comedic madcap zaniness there is a scratching, a tearing; an overwhelming sense of the terror of history bubbling up from below; a profound and wholly justified cosmic rage.

Happy New Year! Starting Pedro Páramo by Juan Rulfo, translated from the Spanish by Douglas J. Weatherford. First book of the year. For newly formed novella book club. And because Sontag called it “one of the masterpieces of twentieth-century world literature.”
